{{Short description|Mathematical model to quantify lift}}
The '''Lanchester–Prandtl lifting-line theory'''<ref name=Anderson>Anderson, John D. (2001), ''Fundamentals of Aerodynamics'', p.&nbsp;360. McGraw-Hill, Boston. {{ISBN|0-07-237335-0}}.</ref> is a mathematical model in [[aerodynamics]] that predicts [[Lift (force)|lift]] distribution over a three-dimensional [[wing]] from the wing's [[Shape|geometry]].<ref name=A4ES>{{cite book |author1=Houghton, E. L. |title=Aerodynamics for Engineering Students |author2=Carpenter, P. W. |year=2003 |isbn=0-7506-5111-3 |editor=Butterworth Heinmann |edition=5th}}</ref>  The theory was expressed independently<ref name=KarmanHist>{{cite book |last=von&nbsp;Kármán|first=Theodore |title=Aerodynamics: Selected Topics in the Light of their Historical Development |orig-year=1954 |isbn=0-486-43485-0 |publisher=Dover |year=2004 |author-link=Theodore von Kármán}}</ref> by [[Frederick W. Lanchester]] in 1907,<ref name=Lanc07>{{cite book |author=Lanchester, Frederick W. |url=https://archive.org/details/aerodynamicscons00lanc |title=Aerodynamics |year=1907 |editor=Constable |author-link=Frederick W. Lanchester}}</ref> and by [[Ludwig Prandtl]] in 1918–1919<ref name=Prandtl18>{{cite book |author=Prandtl, Ludwig |title=Tragflügeltheorie |year=1918 |editor=Königliche Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen |author-link=Ludwig Prandtl}}</ref> after working with [[Albert Betz]] and [[Max Munk]].  In this model, the vortex bound to the wing develops along the whole wingspan because it is shed as a vortex-sheet from the trailing edge, rather than just as a single vortex from the wing-tips.<ref>[[Ira H. Abbott|Abbott, Ira H.]], and Von Doenhoff, Albert E., ''Theory of Wing Sections'', Section 1.4.</ref><ref>Clancy, L. J., ''Aerodynamics'', Section 8.11.</ref>

==Introduction==
[[File:1915ca_laminar_fluegel(cropped).jpg|thumb|Airfoils in two dimensions are easier to understand, but they do not directly map to three-dimensional finite wings]]
It is difficult to predict analytically the overall amount of lift that a wing of given geometry will generate.  When analyzing a three-dimensional [[finite wing]], a traditional approach [[Method of lines|slices the wing into cross-sections]] and analyzes each cross-section independently as a wing in a two-dimensional world. Each of these slices is called an [[airfoil]], and it is easier to understand an airfoil than a complete three-dimensional wing.

One might expect that understanding the full wing simply involves adding up the independently calculated forces from each airfoil segment. However, this approximation is grossly incorrect: on a real wing, the lift from each infinitesimal wing section is strongly affected by the airflow over neighboring wing sections.  Lifting-line theory corrects some of the errors in the naive two-dimensional approach by including some interactions between the wing slices.<gallery class="center" widths="300" heights="215">
File:Lift_distribution_over_a_three-dimensional_wing_(1).svg|alt=Diagram of an aircraft wing, with vertical arrows of magnitude decreasing roughly linearly along the span|An unrealistic lift distribution that neglects three-dimensional effects
File:Lift_distribution_over_a_three-dimensional_wing_(2).svg|alt=Diagram of an aircraft wing, with vertical arrows decreasing sharply near the fuselage and the wingtip|The observed lift distribution on a (finite) trapezoidal wing
</gallery>

== Principle and derivation ==
Lifting line theory supposes wings that are [[Aspect ratio (aeronautics)|long and thin]] with negligible [[fuselage]], akin to a thin bar (the eponymous "lifting line") of [[Wingspan|span]]&nbsp;{{Math|2''s''}} driven through the fluid.  From the [[Kutta–Joukowski theorem]], the lift&nbsp;{{Math|''L''(''y'')}} on a 2-dimensional segment of the wing at distance&nbsp;{{Mvar|y}} from the [[fuselage]] is proportional to the [[circulation (fluid dynamics)|circulation]]&nbsp;{{Math|&Gamma;(''y'')}} about the bar at {{Mvar|y}}.  When the aircraft is stationary on the ground, these circulations are all equal, but when the craft is in motion, they vary with {{Mvar|y}}.  By [[Helmholtz's theorems]], the generation of spatially-varying circulation must correspond to shedding [[Horseshoe vortex|an equal-strength vortex filament downstream from the wing]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Batchelor |first=G.&nbsp;K. |title=An Introduction to Fluid Dynamics |year=1993 |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |isbn=978-81-85618-24-1 |edition=3rd Indian reprint |location=New Delhi |publication-date=2014 |pages=580–585 |language=en-gb |orig-date=1967}}</ref>
{{Gallery|File:Lifting line theory illustration (1).svg|The lift distribution over a wing can be modeled with the concept of [[circulation (fluid dynamics)|circulation]]|File:Lifting line theory illustration (2).svg|[[Horseshoe vortex|A vortex is shed downstream]] for every span-wise change in lift|width=300|align=center}}

In the lifting line theory, the resulting vortex line is presumed to remain [[Horseshoe vortex|bound to the wing]], so that it changes the effective vertical angle of the incoming [[freestream]] air.
{{Gallery|File:Lifting line theory illustration (3).svg|The shed vortex can be modeled as a vertical velocity distribution|File:Lifting line theory illustration (4).svg|The upwash and downwash induced by the shed vortex can be computed at each neighbor segment.|width=300|align=center}}

The vertical motion induced by a vortex line of strength&nbsp;{{Math|&gamma;}} on air a distance&nbsp;{{Mvar|r}} away is {{Math|{{frac|&gamma;|4&pi;''r''}}}}, so that the entire vortex system induces a freestream vertical motion at position&nbsp;{{Mvar|y}} of <math display="block"> w(y)=\int_{-s}^s{\frac{d\Gamma(\tilde{y})}{4\pi(y-\tilde{y})}},</math> where the integral is understood in the sense of a [[Cauchy principal value]].  This flow changes the effective [[angle of attack]] at {{Mvar|y}}; if the circulation response of the airfoils comprising the wing are understood over a range of attack angles, then one can develop an [[integral equation]] to determine {{Math|&Gamma;(''y'')}}.{{Sfn|Batchelor|1993|pp=585–586}}

Formally, there is some angle of orientation such that the airfoil at position&nbsp;{{Mvar|y}} develops no lift.  For airstreams of velocity&nbsp;{{Mvar|V}} oriented at an angle {{Math|&alpha;}} relative to the liftless angle, the airfoil will develop some circulation {{Math|''V''&sdot;''C''(''y'',&alpha;)}}; for small {{Math|&alpha;}}, [[Taylor expansion]] approximates that circulation as {{Math|''V''&sdot;{{frac|&part;''C''|&part;&alpha;}}(''y'',0)&sdot;&alpha;}}.  If the airfoil is ideal and has chord {{Math|''c''(''y'')}}, then [[Kutta condition|theory]] predicts that <math display="block"> C(y,\alpha)=2\pi c(y)\sin(\alpha)\text{,}</math> but real airfoils may be less efficient.<ref name="Acheson">{{cite book |last=Acheson |first=D.&nbsp;J. |title=Elementary Fluid Dynamics |date=1990 |publisher=Clarendon Press |series=Oxford Applied Mathematics and Computing Science |location=Oxford |publication-date=2009 |pages=134–136, 138}}</ref><ref name="A4S">{{cite book |last1=Auld |first1=Douglass |url=http://www.aerodynamics4students.com/ |title=Aerodynamics for Students |last2=Srinivas |publisher=University of Sydney |year=1995 |chapter=3-D Lifting Line Theory |chapter-url=http://www.aerodynamics4students.com/subsonic-aerofoil-and-wing-theory/3d-prandtl-lifting-line-theory.php}}</ref>

Suppose the freestream flow attacks the airfoil at position&nbsp;{{Mvar|y}} at angle {{Math|&alpha;(''y'')}} (relative to the liftless angle for the airfoil at position {{Mvar|y}}&nbsp;— thus a uniform flow across a wing may still have varying {{Math|&alpha;(''y'')}}).  By the [[small-angle approximation]], the effective angle of attack at {{Mvar|y}} of the combined freestream and vortex system is {{Mvar|&alpha;(''y'')+{{frac|''w''(''y'')|''V''}}}}.  Combining the above formulae,{{NumBlk||<math display="block"> \begin{align}
\Gamma(y)&=V\cdot\frac{\partial C}{\partial\alpha}(y,0)\left(\alpha(y)+\frac{w(y)}{V}\right) \\
&=\partial_\alpha C(y,0)\left(V\alpha(y)+\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{-s}^s{\frac{\Gamma'(\tilde{y})\,dy}{y-\tilde{y}}}\right)\text{.}
\end{align}</math>|{{EqRef|1}}}}  All the quantities in this equation except {{Mvar|V}} and {{Math|&Gamma;}} are geometric properties of the wing, and so an engineer can (in principle) solve for {{Math|&Gamma;(''y'')}} given a fixed {{Mvar|V}}.  As in the derivation of [[thin-airfoil theory]], a common approach is to expand {{Math|&Gamma;}} as a Fourier series along the wing, and then keep only the first few terms.{{Sfn|Batchelor|1993|pp=586–587}}<ref name=RollTwist>{{Citation |last1=Phillips |first1=Warren |chapter=Lifting-Line Analysis of Roll Control and Variable Twist |date=2003-06-23 |chapter-url=https://arc.aiaa.org/doi/10.2514/6.2003-4061 |title=21st AIAA Applied Aerodynamics Conference |access-date=2020-12-02 |series=Fluid Dynamics and Co-located Conferences |publisher=American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics |doi=10.2514/6.2003-4061 |isbn=978-1-62410-092-5 |last2=Alley |first2=Nicholas |last3=Goodrich |first3=Wayne|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=TwistSep>{{Cite journal |last=Phillips |first=W. F. |date=2004-01-01 |title=Lifting-Line Analysis for Twisted Wings and Washout-Optimized Wings |url=https://arc.aiaa.org/doi/10.2514/1.262 |journal=Journal of Aircraft |volume=41 |issue=1 |pages=128–136 |doi=10.2514/1.262|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Once the velocity {{Mvar|V}}, circulation {{Math|&Gamma;}}, and fluid density&nbsp;{{Math|&rho;}} are known, the lift generated by the wing is assumed to be the net lift produced by each airfoil with the prescribed circulation... <math display="block"> L=\rho V\int_{-s}^s{\Gamma(y)\,dy} </math> ...and the drag is likewise the total across airfoils: <math display="block">D=\rho V\int_{-s}^s{\Gamma(y)\alpha(y)\,dy}\text{.}</math>  From these quantities and the aspect ratio {{Math|A&zwj;R}}, the [[Oswald efficiency number#Comparison with span efficiency factor|span efficiency factor]] <math display="block"> e=\frac{1}{\pi\mathrm{A\!R}}\cdot\frac{L^2}{\rho VD}</math>may be computed.<ref>Abbott, Ira H., and Von Doenhoff, Albert E., ''Theory of Wing Sections'', Section 1.3</ref><ref>Clancy, L.J., ''Aerodynamics'', Equation 5.7</ref><ref name=A4S />

== Effects of control inputs ==
[[Flight control surfaces|Control surface]] deflection changes the shape of each airfoil slice, which can produce a different angle-of-no-lift for that airfoil, as well as a different angle-of-attack response.  These do not require substantial modification to the theory, only changing {{Math|&part;<sub>&alpha;</sub>''C''(''y'',0)}} and {{Math|&alpha;(''y'')}} in {{EqNote|1}}.  However, a body with rapidly moving wings, such as a rolling aircraft or flapping bird, experiences a vertical flow across the wing due to the wing's change in orientation, which appears as a missing term in the theory.

===Rolling wings===
When the aircraft is rolling at rate {{Mvar|p}} about the fuselage, an airfoil at ([[Sign (mathematics)|signed]]) position {{Mvar|y}} experiences a vertical airflow at rate {{Math|''py''}}, which correspondingly adds {{Math|{{frac|''py''|''V''}}}} to the effective angle of attack.  Thus {{EqNote|1}} becomes: <math display="block">\Gamma(y)=\partial_\alpha C(y,0)\left(V\alpha(y)+py+\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{-s}^s{\frac{\Gamma'(\tilde{y})\,dy}{y-\tilde{y}}}\right)\text{,}</math>which correspondingly modifies both the lift and the induced drag.<ref name="Flapping">{{Cite journal |last=Phillips |first=W. F. |date=2014-02-28 |title=Analytical Decomposition of Wing Roll and Flapping Using Lifting-Line Theory |url=https://arc.aiaa.org/doi/10.2514/1.C032399 |journal=Journal of Aircraft |volume=51 |issue=3 |pages=761–778 |doi=10.2514/1.C032399|url-access=subscription }}</ref>  This "drag force" comprises the main production of thrust for flapping wings.<ref name=Flapping />

==Elliptical wings==
The [[Oswald efficiency|efficiency]] {{mvar|e}} is theoretically optimized in an elliptical wing with no twist, in which <math display="block">\begin{align}
y&=s\cos\theta \\
c(y)&=\mathrm{A\!R}\,s\sin\theta\text{,}  
\end{align}</math> where {{math|&theta;}} is an alternate parameterization of station along the wing.  For such a wing,<math display=block>e = 1\text{,}</math>which yields the equation for the elliptic induced drag coefficient:<math display=block> C_{D_{induced}} = \frac{C_L^2}{\pi A\!R} </math>According to lifting-line theory, any wing planform can achieve the same efficiency through twist (a position-varying increase in [[Pitch (aviation)|pitch]]) relative to the fuselage.<ref name="TwistSep" />

==Useful approximations==
A useful approximation for the 3D [[lift coefficient]] for elliptical circulation distribution{{citation needed|date=August 2019}} is<math display="block"> \ C_{L} = \partial_\alpha C(0,0)\left(1+\frac{2}{\mathrm{A\!R}}\right)^{-1}\alpha </math>Note that this equation becomes the [[Thin Airfoil Theory|thin airfoil]] equation if ''AR'' goes to infinity.<ref name="AW136">{{cite web |last=Scott |first=Jeff |date=10 August 2003 |title=Question #136: Lift Coefficient & Thin Airfoil Theory |url=http://www.aerospaceweb.org/question/aerodynamics/q0136.shtml |publisher=Aerospaceweb.org |department=Ask a Rocket Scientist: Aerodynamics}}</ref>{{Failed verification|date=April 2023}}

==Limitations==
The lifting line theory does not take into account [[Compressible flow|compression of the air]] by the wings, [[Very viscous flow|viscous flow]] within the fuselage's [[boundary layer]], or wing shapes other than the long, straight and thin, such as [[Swept wing|swept]] or low–[[Aspect ratio (aeronautics)|aspect-ratio]] wings.  The theory also presupposes that flow around the wings is in [[Steady flow|equilibrium]], and does not address bodies that are quickly accelerated relative to the freestream air.
